asprey_2000_monod_kinetics.name: Monod kinetics
asprey_2000_monod_kinetics.description: The model describes baker’s yeast fermentation in a fed-batch reactor, predicting biomass and substrate concentrations over time. It combines reactor component balances with a Monod-type rate law for substrate consumption; the biomass and substrate balances account for growth, dilution, biomass loss, and substrate supplied in the feed. The process is represented by adjustable dilution and feed-substrate concentration profiles, with specified initial concentrations. The paper demonstrates model checking and experiment design using simulated response data with added measurement error, rather than reported measurements from a physical reactor. The authors use the example to test identifiability, distinguish the Monod model from a Canoid alternative, and design experiments for model discrimination and improved parameter precision.

facts.text: The model is for fermentation of baker’s yeast in a fed-batch reactor.
facts.quote: Consider a fed-batch reactor (see Fig. 3) in which the fermentation of baker's yeast is carried out.

facts.text: The paper gives no reactor volume or physical scale for the example.
The process has two time-varying controls: dilution factor and substrate concentration in the feed.
The dilution factor is allowed to range from 0.05 to 0.20 h⁻¹.
The substrate concentration in the feed is allowed to range from 5 to 35 g l⁻¹.
The initial biomass concentration can be chosen between 1 and 10 g l⁻¹.
The initial substrate concentration is fixed at 0.01 g l⁻¹ and cannot be manipulated in the experiment design.
The model has two concentration states, biomass concentration and substrate concentration, and both are measured responses.
The example is a dynamic model with two differential component balances and an algebraic rate law.

facts.text: The paper identifies the measured quantities as biomass and substrate concentrations but does not state the measurement instrument or assay.
The model-discrimination design uses ten sampling times and five control-vector-parameterization intervals for each of the two inputs.
The optimized model-discrimination experiment lasts 40 h, and both responses are sampled at the same selected times.
facts.quote: The optimal experiment lasts 40 h and vertical arrows along the abscissa show the optimal sampling points of the two response variables (both measured at the same sampling points).

facts.text: The model-discrimination experiment improves the reported divergence criterion from an initial value of 1.98 to an optimal value of 1.19 × 10⁵.
facts.quote: giving an optimal divergence of 1.19 × 10⁵

facts.text: The paper tests structural identifiability over a 40 h horizon using a five-element piecewise-constant input parameterization and parameter values in [0.01, 0.98].
Under that test, the reported identifiability objective is 1.166 × 10⁻⁶, below the 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ tolerance, and the paper concludes the tested model is globally identifiable.
Under the same test conditions, the Monod and Canoid models are reported as distinguishable, with a value of 0.339 exceeding the 0.004 threshold.

The paper concludes that the Monod model is better suited to the simulated data based on multiresponse chi-square lack-of-fit analysis, although both candidate models describe the data statistically well.
The lack-of-fit table reports values of 0.58 for the Monod model and 1.96 for the Canoid model, against a reference chi-square value of 26.3.
For improving parameter precision, the paper applies an E-optimal design to the Monod model using the parameter estimates obtained after the discrimination experiment.
facts.quote: Using the estimates shown in Table 1, an experiment design for improving parameter precision using the E-optimality criterion with Eq. (12) was performed.

facts.text: The E-optimal criterion rises from 6.41 × 10⁻⁶ to 14.3 in the designed precision-improvement experiment.
The paper reports that confidence intervals were reduced by an average of 23.0% after the sequentially designed precision-improvement experiment.
facts.quote: the confidence intervals have been reduced on average by 23.0% by using the designed experiments.

facts.text: The example demonstrates design over a maximum experiment duration of 40 h and within the stated ranges for inoculation, dilution, and feed substrate concentration.
facts.quote: A dynamic experiment design was then carried out for model discrimination using Eq. (6) and piece-wise constant control inputs, with a maximum experiment duration of 40 h.

facts.text: The paper uses control vector parameterization to represent time-varying inputs, including piecewise-constant profiles in the bioreactor example.
facts.quote: To mathematically represent time-varying external controls to the process, we use the control vector parameterisation (CVP) technique, with either piecewise constant, or higher-order functions

facts.text: The paper's identifiability and distinguishability tests are formulated as optimization problems, including semi-infinite and max-min problems.
facts.quote: A novel optimisation-based approach is introduced for testing of model structural identifiability and distinguishability, involving semi-infinite programming and max-min problems.

facts.text: The dynamic model-discrimination criterion builds on the Hunter–Reiner approach, whose extension to dynamic experiments was first attempted by Espie and Macchietto (1989).
facts.quote: Espie and Macchietto (1989) were the first to attempt an extension of the Hunter and Reiner (1965) criterion to the dynamic case

facts.text: For dynamic parameter-precision design, the paper discusses Espie and Macchietto (1989), Körkel et al. (1999), and Zullo (1991), and states that its work to date is based largely on Zullo’s criterion.
facts.quote: Much of our work to date is based on a unique criterion put forth by Zullo (1991)

facts.text: The robust optimal-design methods for dynamic experiments are described further in Asprey et al. (2000).
facts.quote: Extensions of this criterion to account for the uncertainty in the point estimates of the parameters are made in Asprey et al. (2000)

facts.text: The Monod fermentation model serves as an example for demonstrating tools for dynamic model building and statistical verification, rather than as a standalone validated production model.
facts.quote: Application of several of the tools was carried out using a typical biochemical application, demonstrating their effectiveness in aiding to build a dynamic process model.

facts.text: The paper does not state that code or reusable data for the bioreactor model are available.

asprey_2000_contois_kinetics.name: Contois kinetics
asprey_2000_contois_kinetics.description: The model represents baker’s yeast fermentation in a fed-batch reactor, using the paper’s second, Canoid-type kinetic alternative, identified here as Contois kinetics. It predicts changes in biomass and substrate concentrations from shared reactor balances and a substrate-consumption rate that depends on the kinetic model. The process is run by varying dilution and the substrate concentration in the feed, with inoculum size also available as an experimental design choice. The paper demonstrates the model-building procedure using simulated response data rather than measurements from a fermentation experiment. The example compares this model with a Monod-kinetics alternative and uses the comparison to demonstrate structural testing and dynamic experiment design for model discrimination.
